# HTML Descriptor Creation Migration Notes

This page preserves a migration check that started from an old file entry point. It did not produce a new file mapping table, and readers will still first encounter the old assessment that treated `js/Storage.js` as the main entry point.

## Paths Retained from the Old Records

The original search started with six terms:`controller`,`storage`,`html`,`createhtmlfile`,`descriptor`,`save`. The search results pointed to `internal/sozi-desktop` at revision `v_prev`,`js/Storage.js`. Based on this, the initial draft set out a straightforward sequence: first examine how Controller enters Storage, then examine how the save operation connects to the HTML file descriptor, and finally look for the objects involved in subsequent reads or exports.

This sequence remained useful later, but "issue names and call names can lead to the file" was written up as a stronger claim: Storage is the main entry point for descriptor creation. That old assessment is retained here. It has no complete call chain, does not record which return value hands off the descriptor, and does not explain whether `save` here means saving state or saving the HTML file. The missing parts must not be filled in as migration results just because the filename and search terms are adjacent.

The content visible at the top of `js/Storage.js` at the time was:

```js
import {SVGDocumentWrapper} from "./svg/SVGDocumentWrapper";
import {backendList} from "./backend/AbstractBackend";
import {EventEmitter} from "events";
import nunjucks from "nunjucks";
```

These four lines split further reading into several adjacent objects.`SVGDocumentWrapper` points to the SVG document wrapper,`backendList` points to the backend list,`EventEmitter` points to the event mechanism, and `nunjucks` points to the template engine. They are all merely direct dependencies already visible in the file. The page does not contain enough snippets to prove that any one of them actually creates the HTML descriptor, nor enough to establish their order in the save path.

## The Migration Sequence at the Time

The old page recorded the process as "use the issue name to find the file, then continue following the save term". In practice, the first step was to pin down the repository and revision, open `js/Storage.js`, and copy the dependencies at the top of the file into a separate record; then look up `descriptor` to confirm where the HTML file descriptor information appears; then look up `save` to see whether the save operation passes that information to the next piece of logic. If the calls between Controller and Storage could be traced further, the last visible call target was to be retained, rather than substituting a new function name based on the issue name.

The explanation at the time placed descriptor creation early in the save chain. Therefore, as long as the save operation could still be traced further, the old page tended to treat subsequent objects as part of the same migration route. This was a working hypothesis in the old material, not a relationship confirmed later. It did not record the actual caller, nor did it retain snippets showing the construction or return of the descriptor object.

The diagram below reconstructs only the two ends that the old page could identify; the right side deliberately does not supply a plausible-looking new file:

```text
Old issue name / call name
        |
        v
internal/sozi-desktop @ v_prev
        |
        v
js/Storage.js
        |
        +-- SVGDocumentWrapper
        +-- backendList
        +-- EventEmitter
        +-- nunjucks
        |
        +-- descriptor / save: Continue checking

Post-migration file-level destination: Not recorded
Actual creation location of the HTML descriptor: Unconfirmed
```

The four dependencies in the diagram come from the top of the file, and do not mean that all four jointly form the descriptor creation process.`descriptor` and `save` are lookup targets retained from the old investigation; they can help return to the original reading position, but cannot by themselves answer "who creates the descriptor" or "who passes it to the export operation".

## Differences Identified by the Follow-up Review

The follow-up review treated "locating the file" and "confirming relationships" separately. It first used the old search terms to reach the same revision, then checked whether the file declarations and save operation could be connected within the available snippets. The review still established only `js/Storage.js` and its dependencies at the top of the file, without producing a new target path, and without enough material to turn the old assessment about Storage into a current conclusion.

The only information from the old side that can therefore be retained is:

| Item | Old page record |
| --- | --- |
| Repository | `internal/sozi-desktop` |
| revision | `v_prev` |
| File | `js/Storage.js` |
| Entry method | The HTML descriptor issue name and related call names |
| Working assessment | Storage is the main entry point for further checks on descriptor creation |
| Observed dependencies | `SVGDocumentWrapper`,`backendList`,`EventEmitter`,`nunjucks` |
|

The "working assessment" in the table does not mean that the old files have already been replaced by the new ones. No filenames, function names or callers are recorded for the new side, so none of the four import statements can be designated as the migration target.

## Where Retracing the Old Page Leads

If the original search needs to be reproduced, first return to `js/Storage.js` in `v_prev`, then examine the two local objects `descriptor` and `save` separately. First examine where `descriptor` appears, and record whether it is created, read or merely passed through as an argument; then examine where `save` appears, and record what type of object is being saved. The old page did not retain enough code snippets to determine these actions, so verbs cannot be supplied here to fill in those gaps.

If the only confirmed fact is that Controller has entered Storage, use that point as the current endpoint. Do not infer from `nunjucks` that template rendering is descriptor creation, or infer from `EventEmitter` that emitting an event means saving is complete. The former appears only at the top of the file, and the latter only shows that the file uses an event mechanism. Likewise,`SVGDocumentWrapper` and `backendList` show only the direction of local dependencies, not the handoff order of the HTML file descriptor information.

If later snippets show that the HTML file descriptor information continues to be passed to another object, the migration record must at least retain the recipient, the location where the handoff occurs and the location of the save operation together. The old page did not retain these names; therefore the only action currently available is to continue checking the open revision, and write down the last confirmed object. "We have seen descriptor" must not be recorded as "we have found the creation point for descriptor".

Migration batches were not recorded either. There is no batch number, target file or item-by-item record of replacements between the old and new interfaces here, so no batch may be invented based on the topic of R2026.09. If the page lands on Storage again from the same set of terms, first compare the repository, revision and the actual context in which `save` appears; unless all three match, the old page can only serve as a historical entry point.

## Restoring the Old Path

The path that can be restored from the old page is very narrow: reopen `v_prev`,`js/Storage.js` from `internal/sozi-desktop`, then start again with the same set of search terms. This can restore the original reading context, but cannot prove that this is still the current implementation, nor can it produce an unrecorded new call chain.

When restoring the path, retain the original record of the dependencies at the top of the file. They help distinguish four kinds of adjacent dependency involving the SVG document wrapper, the backend list, the event emitter and the template engine, but this page has no further material explaining which occurs before the save operation. If only these import statements remain, the migration stops at the file level; if only the entry from Controller into Storage has been seen, the migration stops at the call entry point level. Both stopping points are closer to the old record than filling in a guessed target file.

`SOZI-212` serves only as navigation for the "HTML Descriptor Creation" user flow. Later actions linked it to this page, with the purpose of returning to the actual flow to check for missing steps, not retroactively writing the card content into the old page as confirmed source-code relationships. Related material on save timing can be found at `DOC-20`; this page does not incorporate that material's assessments into the descriptor migration.

## Points That Remain Unresolved

- The function or object that actually creates the HTML descriptor has not been recorded.
- There is no file-level destination for the migration from `js/Storage.js`.
- The return-value handoffs between Controller, Storage and the descriptor have not been retained.
- The object boundaries of `save` were not clearly separated in the old snippets.
- There are not enough snippets to explain whether an asynchronous gap exists between descriptor availability and save completion.
- No mapping has been produced for the post-migration caller, batch and specific restoration actions.

These gaps are retained alongside the old assessment. The old page said Storage was the main entry point, and the review only restored that claim to the status of a working assessment that still needs verification; the review did not replace it with another unrecorded entry point. If this page is expanded further, the first things needed are the actual creation location and the recipient, not more issue names or dependencies from the top of the file.

## Appendix of Old Examples

**Opening a file based only on the issue name.** After searching for `html` and `descriptor` and landing on `js/Storage.js`, the old page immediately began writing migration steps. This example explains how the old entry point came about, and also preserves the mistake of treating file location as relationship confirmation. When retracing the search, at least keep the revision together with the last actual call target.

**Treating an import as the next stop.** Treating template rendering as the next step in descriptor creation upon seeing `nunjucks`, or treating an event notification as save completion upon seeing `EventEmitter`, are both accounts unsupported by call snippets. They remain in the appendix because these are precisely the assessments the old page may have left behind; they are not polished here into current migration steps.

**Treating `save` as the same operation.** The old sequence checked `descriptor` and `save` side by side, but did not record the object saved by `save`. If later inspection shows only state being saved without showing the HTML file descriptor information, the account cannot continue along the old hypothesis. This example is retained to show that identical search terms do not imply identical object handoffs.

# DevTools Frame Screenshot Decision Record

When this record was first created, both the issue name and the call name would lead people to `Gruntfile.js`. At the time, there was a convenient inference: since the old investigation always started here, DevTools Frame Screenshots probably also used this as its primary implementation entry point. This inference is suitable as a starting point for searches, but not as an implementation conclusion in long-term documentation.

After reviewing the file itself, very little can be seen directly. The file header contains `require("load-grunt-tasks")(grunt);`; the repository index lists it as an existing js module for code reading and historical behavior verification. Both pieces of information show that this path is worth retaining, but neither shows that frame screenshots, image data, or PNG processing is performed here. The initial draft placed "can start investigating here" too close to "this is responsible for screenshots," making it easy to read the former as the latter.

The decision recorded here is not to specify a new implementation approach for DevTools Frame Screenshots. It addresses a narrower issue: when an old investigation path has entered the long-term knowledge base, but local file facts are insufficient to determine implementation ownership, what should be retained, what should be explicitly ruled out, and where subsequent verification should continue.

## Retain the old judgment, but no longer use it

The merit of the old judgment is that it did not discard the historical entry point. DevTools Frame Screenshots was not a term that appeared out of nowhere in public materials; the old investigation once linked it to `Gruntfile.js` using the issue name and call name. If later readers see only the wording in release notes, user documentation, or templates, they cannot know where the earlier search began; if they retain only a generic "check export," they lose the specific path back to the old revision.

The problem with the old judgment is that it treated the file location as the behavior location. A build file being hit by old clues does not mean that it owns the screenshot module boundary; a statement in the file header that loads a Grunt task does not mean that the screenshot operation is initiated by that file. The earlier wording did not clearly separate these two levels, leaving maintainers with a misleading shortcut: once they found `Gruntfile.js`, it seemed they had also found the implementation of DevTools Frame Screenshots.

This shortcut is now retired. What is retired is the inference that "`Gruntfile.js` is the primary implementation entry point for screenshots," not the path itself. The path remains as a historical navigation point, and the old investigation can still use it to return to the code location at that time; however, no new conclusion may be drawn solely from the path, filename, or a single `require` statement.

## Handling options considered at the time

There were three options during the initial draft.

| Handling approach | What it could solve at the time | Reason or cost for abandoning it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Consistently state `Gruntfile.js` as the screenshot implementation entry point | The old investigation could be reused directly, and the reading path was shortest | The visible contents of the file could not support this ownership; if references were later found elsewhere, the old conclusion would mislead the scope of changes to public materials |
| Delete `Gruntfile.js` and retain only "check export" | Avoid describing the build file as the screenshot module | This would erase the search trail formed by the old issue name and call name, preventing later readers from understanding where the history began |
| Limit the path to a recheck entry point and continue confirming the relationship through revision references | Retain the historical clue without prematurely defining the implementation boundary | Verification cannot end at the filename; public wording checks and code relationship checks need to be recorded separately |

The third option was chosen. The focus of this decision is the "limitation." `Gruntfile.js` was not elevated to an authoritative behavior description, nor was it removed because the relationship had not yet been fully expanded. Its retained role is to take readers back to the starting point used by the old investigation and remind them not to miswrite that starting point as the implementation endpoint.

This is especially important for Quality and Regression materials. The name of the screenshot capability may appear both in public wording and in code-reading clues. Public wording is concerned with whether the external description is consistent; code rechecking is concerned with whether the actual references at the time support that description. The two kinds of work may encounter the same term, but they should not mutually prove one another through the same unconfirmed chain.

## The two workstreams separated in this review

The first workstream is public wording. The maintenance scope of SOZI-217 has been defined as checking the current wording of "DevTools Frame Screenshots" in the release notes, user documentation, and templates, and listing the specific files that need modification. The objects here are three categories of public materials, not an abstract description of the screenshot architecture. Recording specific filenames is intended to keep the modification work moving, not to infer a code module from the names of the materials.

The second workstream is historical behavior rechecking. The old investigation placed the entry point in `internal/sozi-desktop`'s `v_prev` revision, at `Gruntfile.js`. This workstream needs to inspect the actual references within that revision related to export, screenshot data, and PNG. It answers whether the old clues can support a more specific module relationship, not whether the release notes have already been updated.

The two workstreams can proceed in parallel, but their outputs differ. The public wording check produces release notes, user documentation, and template files that need revision or confirmation; the historical behavior recheck produces relationships between the path and references that can be confirmed. The former cannot declare where the screenshot implementation is, and the latter cannot declare that all public files have been processed.

SOZI-217 entered the actual review-and-edit stage after the interface review was completed, showing that the maintenance work had progressed from "whether a check is needed" to "starting the check and modification." This does not prove that every piece of public wording has been adjusted, much less that the responsibilities of `Gruntfile.js` have expanded or contracted. The record retains only this status change and does not turn an unprovided file list or completion result into an established fact.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Old investigation lead
    Old investigation lead --> Gruntfile recheck entry
    Gruntfile recheck entry --> Revision reference check
    Revision reference check --> Confirmed relationship
    Revision reference check --> Navigation relationship only
    Confirmed relationship --> Public wording check
    Navigation relationship only --> Public wording check
    Public wording check --> Release notes
    Public wording check --> User documentation
    Public wording check --> Templates
```

The states in the diagram are not a call sequence, nor do they indicate that `Gruntfile.js` will execute these operations one after another. They only describe how this record should handle the existing materials: the old investigation provides the path first, references in the revision determine whether a module relationship can be stated, and the public materials form a separate maintenance scope that needs checking. These states are shown together to prevent "the path appeared" from being read as "the behavior was confirmed."

## Responsibility boundaries

This page covers historical interpretation and the decision record. It preserves the initial draft's misreading, the limitation adopted after review, and the boundary that public wording and historical rechecking must not be mixed. It does not provide the exporter's interface documentation, nor does it store the final wording for the release notes, user documentation, or templates.

`Gruntfile.js` covers only the currently confirmed local facts: it belongs to an existing js module; the file header uses `require("load-grunt-tasks")(grunt);` to load Grunt tasks; and the old investigation led DevTools Frame Screenshots here from the issue name and call name. Further responsibilities, such as how the screenshot response is obtained, how PNG is generated, or which location is responsible for handing the image to the export flow, must all be supported by actual references in that revision.

SOZI-217 handles maintenance navigation. The card says to look at the release notes, user documentation, and templates, and requires listing the specific files that need modification. The card does not designate these three types of materials as evidence of code ownership, so this page does not connect them into a chain "from the build file to the user interface." Public wording can express a capability, but wording alone cannot confirm the responsibilities in the build file.

DOC-22 remains associated with this page because both are local materials from the same development wrap-up phase; this page does not infer from that association that Hardware Acceleration Startup Toggle and frame screenshots share the same implementation path. Related documents provide navigation; they do not replace the evidence scope of the current decision.

## Handling two counterexamples

The first counterexample is "the filename explains everything." This reading usually starts from `Gruntfile.js`, then assigns all the export, data, or PNG terms in the old issue name to that file. It ignores that the only directly visible dependency is loading Grunt tasks, and it also ignores that the repository index describes the file's purpose as code reading and historical verification. A filename and search clues can shorten the lookup process, but they cannot alone constitute the boundary of the screenshot implementation.

The second counterexample is "if the relationship has not been fully expanded, the entry point should not be retained." This turns caution into amnesia. The old investigation is worth preserving precisely because it records where the issue was entered at the time; after the path is deleted, readers can see only a requirement name that has lost its starting point. The correct handling is not to delete it, but to state next to the path what it can prove: it is a recheck point for the old record, not evidence that completes the ownership determination.

There is also a more subtle misreading: treating the maintenance scope of the public materials as an implementation checklist. The release notes, user documentation, and templates may all need checking, but each preserves external wording or example content. Even if all three mention DevTools Frame Screenshots, that cannot establish that the screenshot code is located in the build file, or that there are no other related locations in the old revision. The public materials need to be consistent, while the code relationship needs to be investigated separately; that is precisely why the two workstreams were separated.

## Follow-up verification points

When rechecking from `Gruntfile.js`, first retain the visible fact that the file header loads the task, then inspect the references adjacent to the old issue name and call name in the `v_prev` revision. Export, data, and PNG are search terms left by the old investigation, not pre-assumed call-chain nodes. Only when a direct reference appears should it be written as a relationship; if the result is still only build-task adjacency, stop at the level of "navigation relationship confirmed."

Work on the public materials begins with the three types of locations indicated by SOZI-217. The release notes, user documentation, and templates should be checked separately; the wording in one location must not be used to assume that the other two are already consistent. Specific files enter the modification list only after they have been actually checked. The current materials do not provide this list, so the decision does not prefill filenames or describe the start of the work as completion.

This arrangement does not require rewriting all old materials into an end-to-end explanation. A long-term record needs a stable boundary: old clues remain searchable, the explanation of the path cannot go beyond the existing file facts, and revision of the public wording cannot replace confirmation of historical references. Thus, if it is later found that `Gruntfile.js` only handles a narrower build adjacency, only the old "primary implementation entry point" judgment needs to be corrected; the fact that the old investigation began here does not need to be erased.

## Current decision

1. Retain `Gruntfile.js` as the historical recheck entry point for the history of DevTools Frame Screenshots.
2. No longer describe this path as the primary entry point for the screenshot implementation; the filename, old issue name, and a single direct dependency are all insufficient to establish this ownership.
3. Base subsequent explanations of code relationships on the actually visible references in the `internal/sozi-desktop` `v_prev` revision.
4. Check the external maintenance scope separately against the release notes, user documentation, and templates listed by SOZI-217; record the specific files that need modification after the check.
5. The search clues in the old record remain usable, but "previously pointed here" and "handled here" must remain two different judgments.

The initial draft only said, "Retain the path and wait for reference confirmation." The direction was not wrong, but the wording was too broad. The reviewed version adds not more screenshot implementation details, but what can and cannot be done during this waiting period: references can be searched along the old revision, and public materials can be checked item by item; the search entry cannot be expanded into module ownership, and a maintenance action that has started cannot be written as a completed release revision.

The unresolved issue is also retained here: which actual module responsible for frame screenshots the old issue name and call name will ultimately point to can be answered only after the revision references are expanded. Until then, the value of this decision is not to preempt the future result, but to prevent the historical entry point, public wording, and implementation responsibility from being mixed into the same statement again.

# Hardware Acceleration Startup Toggle Proposal

First consolidate the startup switch's implementation point in the Electron backend, then decide whether to expose it through external configuration. The existing verification entry point is `js/backend/Electron.js`; the file shows imports of `AbstractBackend` and `addBackend`, along with `fs`, `path`, and `process`. This is enough to limit the experiment to the area adjacent to backend startup, but not enough to determine which section is responsible for window creation, configuration reading, and backend registration, respectively.

Two implementation points will be compared. The first is to read an explicit startup setting when the Electron backend begins initialization and perform the corresponding handling before the window is created. This keeps the switch adjacent to runtime initialization and lets investigation start from the same file. The tradeoff is that we must confirm the initialization path runs only once; if the same process initializes more than once, repeated handling of the switch must be defined separately.

The second is to put the switch after an existing window or UI action. This option may have a smaller implementation change surface, but it is not suitable as this round's first choice: hardware acceleration is a process startup condition, and a switch made after window creation, even without an error, cannot show that the runtime state actually changed. During the trial phase, we will not present it as an in-editor immediate option.

The experiment will record only three things: where the setting enters the backend, the ordering between the actual execution point and window creation, and whether the same setting produces consistent results across consecutive launches. The import of `process` in the file can serve as a lead for checking startup arguments or the process environment; whether to reuse it and what name to read are not fixed here. `fs` and `path` also cannot be treated as the basis for a settings-file approach merely because they have already been imported.

The withdrawal conditions are straightforward: if reference checking shows that `Electron.js` only handles backend registration, and window creation occurs on another path whose ordering cannot be guaranteed, withdraw the proposal to "host the switch in this file" and first map the initialization call chain; if the switch can only be triggered after the window appears, do not merge it as a startup switch. This round has not yet decided the configuration form, default value, or whether the switch state needs to be shown in the UI.

The next review will compare only two records from the same cold-start path: one with the setting disabled and one explicitly enabled; both must retain timestamps from before and after window creation and the backend logs. If the execution point is later than the first window, or the second launch cannot reproduce the result consistently, return the proposal to call-chain investigation; do not use UI behavior in place of evidence about startup ordering.

versions.body:
# PNG Sequence Write-to-Disk Troubleshooting Tree

Start with the export page the user reaches first. This documents the old troubleshooting sequence for when the PNG sequence is not written to disk as expected; do not treat an old link in a regular directory directly as a write failure.

When the page is still reachable but the sequence cannot be found, first note two things: whether the user clicked the current entry point or a legacy entry point; and whether a new directory appeared alongside the target HTML file after the export action. These checks are not interchangeable. The former only shows that the entry page still exists; the latter is closer to evidence of a write to disk.

```
PNG sequence not found
|
+-- Did the user enter via a legacy directory link?
|   |
|   +-- Yes: Return to the current export entry point and reproduce it once more; do not treat the legacy link itself as a write anomaly yet
|   |
|   +-- No: Continue
|
+-- Did the export action actually start?
|   |
|   +-- No: Stop at the page action; do not check the output directory
|   |
|   +-- Yes: Check the directory alongside the HTML file
|
+-- Did no new content appear in the directory alongside it?
    |
    +-- Yes: Check how tasks are loaded in Gruntfile.js
    |
    +-- No: Keep the directory observation; investigate the sequence contents separately
```

The old record treated `Gruntfile.js` as the first code entry point. At the beginning of the file is:

```js
require("load-grunt-tasks")(grunt);
```

This only shows that the Grunt task gets loaded; the initial draft roughly treated it as a signal that the PNG output task had been wired up. That interpretation is appropriate for the earliest follow-up check, but it cannot by itself show who created the directory or whether every sequence file finished writing.

If the loading statement is not present here, stop and verify the source version being examined; do not continue guessing task names from the old troubleshooting notes. If the loading statement is present, record "task loading visible," then return to the actual disk-write location. Record the page entry, task loading, and directory result separately; otherwise, the next time an expired link and an output anomaly will be treated as the same issue.

Unresolved: If the same-level directory exists but its contents are incomplete, the old record did not leave enough decision points.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Writing PNG Sequences to Disk

This record originally grew out of a report that "the page still opens, but the PNG sequence does not appear in the expected location". The old version focused on `Gruntfile.js`, because the shortest path visible at the time was the task-loading statement. That entry point was not removed during later reviews: it is still useful for looking back at the old build conventions, but it no longer means "the write location has been found".

First describe the observed situation in two separate sentences. The first sentence should state where the user entered the export page from, and the second should state what appeared alongside the HTML file after the export. Do not compress "the page has an export option", "Export was clicked", "the directory does not exist", and "the directory exists but some frames are missing" into a single "PNG export failed". These situations lead to different branches, and old links are especially likely to send people down the wrong branch first.

This page still keeps the starting point very narrow: the page the user first reached. SOZI-222 later added instructions for using this entry point to check pages that are still active and links that are outdated, so troubleshooting starts by asking about the page, not because the page itself is responsible for writing PNG, but to avoid carrying the misleading impression created by the old directory into the subsequent code checks.

---

## Record the State First, Without Rushing to Explain It

When a problem occurs, first record the following four items in the on-call log, in any order, but without mixing their content:

- Whether the user accessed the current export page or an old link in a regular directory;
- Whether the page still allowed further interaction after the click or the action did not start;
- Whether a new directory appeared alongside the target HTML file;
- If the new directory exists, whether it contains no images at all, only some of the images, or the files exist but the user looked in the wrong place.

"Alongside" here means an adjacent location in the filesystem, not the same level in page navigation. In the old notes, someone referred to both the directory page and the file output directory as the "export directory", so every later review required asking again which one they meant. We now keep two distinct terms: an old link in a regular directory refers to an old page the user reached by clicking in the documentation or navigation; a directory alongside the HTML file refers to the actual location where the export action may produce an image sequence.

If you only have the first item, do not open the source code yet. The page entry point may be outdated, but it cannot tell us whether this export ran. Conversely, if you already have the third or fourth item, it is still worth noting whether the page link is outdated, but that should not block an assessment of what happened on disk.

The old version put too much weight on "being able to open the page". That was a convenient check at the time, not a reliable success criterion. Being able to open the page only means the entry point is reachable; it proves neither that the task loaded successfully nor that the image sequence was generated.

---

## Branches Based on the Observed State

The tree below follows a practical order, rather than providing a complete implementation diagram. Each "stop" means the available material only supports going this far, so record the observations and switch entry points, without filling in the gaps with guesses.

```text
PNG sequence did not appear in the expected location
|
+-- A. Where did the user enter from?
|   |
|   +-- An old link in a regular directory
|   |   |
|   |   +-- Return to the current export page and reproduce once
|   |   +-- The current page cannot start the export either: stop at the page action
|   |   `-- The current page can start the export: go to B
|   |
|   `-- The current export page
|       `-- Go to B
|
+-- B. Has the export action started?
|   |
|   +-- It has not started or there is no discernible subsequent change
|   |   `-- Stop at the page action; do not inspect the PNG directory to draw a conclusion about it
|   |
|   `-- It has started
|       `-- Go to C
|
+-- C. Is there a new directory alongside the HTML file?
|   |
|   +-- No
|   |   |
|   |   +-- Verify the Gruntfile.js being viewed
|   |   +-- Only check whether the task-loading statement is visible
|   |   `-- Still no directory after task loading becomes visible: go to the actual write path and do not draw a conclusion on this page
|   |
|   `-- Yes
|       |
|       +-- No image files: preserve the directory state and check the sequence generation boundary
|       +-- Some image files are present: preserve the range already written to disk and check where it stopped midway
|       `-- All image files are present but the consumer cannot find them: recheck where the page or consumer points
|
`-- Cannot distinguish between the page, action, and directory
    `-- Stop; first add a record of something observable in the current situation
```

A and B in the tree are intended to eliminate noise caused by old links. C is where this page's original scope begins: whether the PNG sequence is written to disk. In the past, someone jumped directly from a regular directory page to `Gruntfile.js`, then saw that task loading was normal and described the issue as "The task was not registered". That path lacked evidence connecting the page, task loading, and directory creation, and was retained as a counterexample after review.

### A: First determine whether this is an entry-point issue

The first page the user reaches is a fixed checkpoint in this record. If the entry point is an old link in a regular directory, first re-enter from the current export page, then observe whether the action can start. Old links sometimes still open, so "it opens" cannot be used to determine that a link is still valid; likewise, an old link failing to open does not automatically mean there is a problem with the write boundary of the PNG sequence.

Do not delete or replace the old link just for convenience here. The troubleshooting record needs to retain it, because some people will still enter from there, and this is precisely the most common source of ambiguity in the field. As long as it is still unclear which entry point the user clicked, do not record "No output after export". A more accurate description is "The old entry point did not produce an export action that could be evaluated".

If it is clear that the user came in through the current export page, go straight to B. At this point, there is no need to spend more time proving whether the regular directory link is stale. Entry-point state and sequence writes to disk can both be part of the same incident report, but they are not the same thing.

### B: The stopping point before the action has started

"Not started" includes cases where the page has not entered the post-export state, a click has not produced any discernible subsequent change, or the report from the scene says only "I clicked and didn't see anything". These descriptions are not enough to determine whether PNG was written. What is needed now is to fill in the missing observations of the page action, not infer task failure from a missing directory.

An earlier draft suggested opening the build file at this step. That suggestion was later crossed out, but its original intent is retained: at the time, the investigator had only a code entry point and no page-side records, so task loading was used as a substitute check. We now know that this conflates two layers. When the action has not started, the state of `Gruntfile.js` can at most help confirm whether the old build configuration is readable; it cannot explain that particular click by the user.

At this stopping point, the record can be very brief: the entry location, whether the action started, and whether sibling directories have already been checked. It is fine if the third item is missing. Do not add a statement about whether the directory contains images just to make the record look complete, because that would invent an observation that never took place.

### C: Directory results are what define the write-to-disk branch

Once the export action has started, check whether a new directory appears alongside the target HTML file. Classify only by observation here: no directory, a directory that is empty, a directory containing only some images, or images that appear complete but downstream consumers still cannot find them. Do not guess who created a directory based on its name, and do not record "a directory exists" as "the sequence is complete".

When there is no directory, the old process would immediately say "check Gruntfile". The revised version still puts it in the next step, but with a narrower purpose: to confirm whether the task-loading entry point referred to in the old troubleshooting notes is still in the files currently available for inspection. If the file contents do not match the old notes, stop following those notes for now; at this point, the most useful thing is to point out the mismatch in what is being inspected, rather than guess at a new build relationship.

When a directory exists but contains no image files, do not go back and reopen the page-entry branch. The page may be entirely correct, and the directory may indeed have been created; what is missing is observation of the segment between directory creation and sequence writing. Simply retain the original wording "directory exists, no images seen". This is more honest than "export is halfway successful", because the current material does not define "halfway successful".

When some image files are present, record the range already observed and where it stopped partway through. Do not arbitrarily classify the issue as encoding, rendering, or cleanup here; these terms were casually borrowed in the old discussion, but this page does not have enough material to link the missing frames to any of them. What can be confirmed is that the sequence was not left in the sibling directory as a complete result; what cannot be confirmed is why it stopped at that point.

When all image files are present but the consumer cannot find them, the issue is no longer "whether they were written to disk". Return to the path or page entry point the consumer is looking at. This branch remains in the tree to prevent on-call records from invariably recording "cannot find it" as "not generated". It does not require continuing to investigate the consumer on this page; it only requires stopping judgments about the PNG write boundary.

---

## Legacy build entry point: retain it, but limit your reading to what it can prove

`Gruntfile.js` is the only fixed source-code entry point on this page. The visible direct dependency is:

```js
require("load-grunt-tasks")(grunt);
```

This line of code is suitable as the first file check in the old troubleshooting process. It shows that Grunt loads tasks; when old notes mention "the task is not hooked up," first confirm whether this line is still present; this is a low-cost branch. It also explains why the early records started here rather than with the user page.

However, this line of code does not list the directories in the PNG sequence, does not show when writes occur, and does not provide the completion condition for image files. Reading it as "the PNG task definitely exists" is the clearest overreach in the old page. Later review found no local material sufficient to elevate that inference to a fact, so the new version downgrades it back to "task loading is visible."

The following two short statements are recommended for records, without adding causal speculation:

- "The task-loading statement is visible in `Gruntfile.js`."
- "The task-loading statement described in the old record is not visible in the object currently being inspected; stop making judgments based on that record."

The first statement does not mean "the export configuration is correct"; the second does not mean "the build configuration is wrong." They only determine whether it is still possible to continue reading along the old entry point. Because these two statements were not distinguished in the past, many supplementary notes recorded file existence, statement existence, and actual output existence as the same conclusion.

If the loading statement is visible but the sibling directory still has not appeared, do not repeatedly check the same line. The issue should be handed off here to verification of the actual write path, rather than continuing in this runbook to list task names, commands, or filenames. The old materials did not preserve these objects; inventing one would only cause later people to mistake speculation for a path.

If the loading statement is not visible, do not modify the current file to make it look like it "should be there" and then continue troubleshooting. The revision being checked may differ, or the entry point referenced by the old record may no longer apply. Either way, the stopping point is the same: write this observation back into the current context and find another entry point directly connected to the current output behavior.

---

## Several Misjudgments Left by the Initial Draft

The initial draft's advantage is that it singled out PNG Sequence Disk Output from the vague "the export is wrong"; the problem is that it trusted the build file too much. To show later readers why the tree has so many stopping points, several of the working formulations from that time are retained below.

> The page can be reached, so the export chain is ready.

This statement no longer applies. A reachable page entry point only means that the user reached a page. An old link to an ordinary directory may still open, and the current export page may also still open; neither case answers whether the export action has started, much less whether a sibling directory has been created.

> `load-grunt-tasks` is visible, so the PNG output task should already be hooked up.

This was later retracted. Visible task loading is not proof that the output task exists, much less proof that writing to the directory has completed. It is now treated only as a signal that the old build entry remains readable.

> Not finding the image directory means writing to disk failed.

This statement is also far too broad. The user may have arrived through an old page, may not have triggered an export action, may have checked a location that is not at the same directory level as the HTML file, or the directory and images may both exist while the user keeps looking in the wrong place. Only after the entry point, action, and location have each been recorded does "no new directory" become a usable on-site observation.

These old statements have not been erased from the history because some people still find this page through their keywords. When reading them, treat them as traces of the old troubleshooting sequence, and do not copy them into new incident records.

---

## The revised sequence after a review

The review was not a redesign of the export workflow, but a breakdown of the early material. The added decision sequence is as follows:

1. First confirm how the user reached the page. Record old links to regular directories separately from the current export page.
2. Next confirm whether there was an identifiable export action. If there was no action, do not proceed to checking whether files were written to disk.
3. Only after the action has started, check for a new directory alongside the HTML file.
4. If the directory exists, further distinguish between an empty directory, some images being present, and all images being present but not found.
5. Read `Gruntfile.js` only in the "no directory" branch; the result can only indicate whether task loading is visible.

The purpose of this sequence is not to add forms, but to prevent one observation from carrying two meanings. For example, "the page opens but there is no directory" contains at least three layers of information: the page, the action, and the location; if any one layer is missing, the next step may target the wrong object.

The review also left a related question unresolved: when the directory exists but contains no images, exactly where should the start of sequence generation be observable. The old notes did not leave a corresponding code entry point, and this page does not pretend to have one either. When this occurs, the on-site record should stop at the directory state, and investigation should continue through another directly related verification entry point.

---

## How to write on-call records

The format below is intended to let the next reader continue from the same facts, without requiring every field to be filled in.

**Entry point:** Current export page / old link to a regular directory / unconfirmed.  
**Action:** Started / not started / unconfirmed.  
**Sibling directory:** Has not appeared / has appeared but is empty / some images present / all images present / unconfirmed.  
**Build entry point:** Task-loading statement visible in `Gruntfile.js` / not visible / not checked.  
**Stopping point:** Page action, sibling directory, sequence contents, or a mismatch with the current source-code entry point.

"Unconfirmed" is not a brush-off. It means that layer has not yet been observed, and cannot be filled in using a result from another layer. For example, the page being the current entry point is no substitute for "the action has started"; an empty directory also does not, conversely, prove that the page must be correct. The most common problem with the old records was precisely that these blanks were quietly filled in with inferences.

If the only thing left in the current situation is the sentence "PNG is gone," prioritize filling in the entry point and directory location. If you can determine where the user came from but do not know whether the action has started, stop at B. If the action has started but it is unclear whether the location being inspected is at the same level as the HTML file, establish the location first. Only when all three have answers is it necessary to read the build file.

There is no need to reproduce the entire tree in the record. Just state the two or three nodes actually traversed. For example: "legacy link to an ordinary directory; after switching to the current export page, the action started; no new directory seen alongside the HTML file; task-loading statement visible, so check the write path." This type of record preserves the boundaries and does not treat the build file as the final root cause.

Counterexamples should also be recorded truthfully: "current export page; action started; images present in the sibling directory; the consumer still has not found them." This is not a conclusion about a PNG on-disk write failure, but a case where you should leave this page. Continuing to classify it under the PNG output would make future readers start again from `Gruntfile.js`, wasting time.

---

## Still-usable legacy operations

Although the old version used criteria that were too broad, the following steps are still retained:

- Start from the page the user reached first, rather than starting with a code search;
- In the absence of a sibling directory, open `Gruntfile.js`;
- After seeing `require("load-grunt-tasks")(grunt);`, record the result as task loading visible;
- When the directory exists, preserve the actual state of the directory and images; do not reduce it to "already exported."

The second step must be used only under the following preconditions: the export action has started, and the sibling directory is indeed absent. Without these preconditions, reading the build file is merely an old habit, not a valid branch.

Regarding directory names, old records relied on users' verbal descriptions, so the wording was inconsistent. Now do not judge whether you are in the right location by whether the name looks like an export directory; use "same level as the target HTML file" and whether images actually appear as the criteria. - It has already been confirmed that the sibling directory contains all images, and the issue has shifted to the consumer not finding them;
- The `Gruntfile.js` being viewed can no longer be matched to the old task-loading entry point;

# Decision Record for Temporary Resources and ffmpeg

This record originally placed "Temporary Resource Cleanup" and "ffmpeg Selection and Fallback" side by side because both were raised during the export wrap-up stage. Placing them together was simply a way to organize the issues at the time, not a judgment about implementation responsibility. The initial draft's working assumption was: if the earlier investigation ultimately traced both issues to the same task chain, they could be handled together; if no such connection could be found, they should be split into two separate follow-up investigation points. The initial draft did not confirm which situation applied.

The earlier record used Gruntfile.js as the starting point, which made it easy for later readers to confuse build tasks with runtime export. The only line still directly visible is this one at the top of the file:

```js
require("load-grunt-tasks")(grunt);
```

It shows that the file loads Grunt tasks, but not when temporary directories are created or deleted, where ffmpeg is selected from, or what kind of failure triggers a switch. The initial draft's instruction to "start here and follow the tasks" is retained as a navigation clue; it is no longer treated as evidence of where export is implemented.

The first approach considered at the time was to assign both issues to build tasks. The idea was to follow Gruntfile.js to find adjacent tasks, then describe cleanup and fallback as a single pre-release issue. This approach had the advantage of fewer starting points and a seemingly coherent narrative. Its problem was equally straightforward: a file loading tasks does not mean those tasks perform runtime export. Without snippets of actual invocations, attributing both issues to the build side went beyond what the available material could support.

The second approach was to treat ffmpeg fallback as a consequence of Temporary Resource Cleanup. This judgment once seemed natural: an encoder failure might leave intermediate artifacts behind, making "encoding failed" and "resources were not cleaned up" look like successive stages of the same issue. But the possibility of their occurring together does not mean one action is triggered by the other. If cleanup itself works normally but the encoder outcome from the earlier invocation is not as expected, this wording would obscure the fallback issue; conversely, even if encoding can continue, resources may still not be cleaned up as expected.

The third approach was to preserve their historical relationship on the same page while separating the judgments. The temporary-resource issue asks only whether any resources remain after export and exactly what the cleanup described by the public entry point covers; the ffmpeg issue asks only what selection method the earlier invocation used and what user-visible result remained after fallback. The two issues may share a release context, but clues about one cannot replace evidence about the other.

This review continues with the third decision. It does not split the two topics into two new sets of rules, nor does it declare either one complete. The decision is that subsequent reviews must not draw conclusions about one topic from clues about the other. The old shared title is retained because it accurately reflects why the investigation grouped them together at the time; from this point on, the body no longer treats that title as implying a single execution chain.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Shared history" as history
    state "Temporary Resource Cleanup" as cleanup
    state "ffmpeg Selection and Fallback" as ffmpeg
    state "Unconfirmed" as unknown
    state "Actual invocation still needed" as call
    [*] --> history
    history --> cleanup: Investigate separately
    history --> ffmpeg: Investigate separately
    cleanup --> unknown
    ffmpeg --> call
```

Follow-up on Temporary Resource Cleanup now uses SOZI-221 as the reference point. The observation recorded on that card is that the current public entry point supports Temporary Resource Cleanup; the same review also explicitly identified one point that remained unconfirmed. Here, "supports" is only enough to establish that this capability exists at the entry-point level, and cannot substitute for confirming what is cleaned up, when deletion occurs, or what is left behind. After the risk review, the card was still moved to In Progress, so the existence of the entry point should not be taken to mean that this issue is closed.

This unconfirmed point is worth keeping separate. The earlier record did not clearly state which type of temporary resource it concerned, nor did it provide samples of leftover resources on which to base a judgment. Extending "the entry point supports cleanup" to "all temporary export resources will be deleted" would turn a scope that was not preserved in the record into a conclusion. At this stage, it can only remain on the cleanup side: confirming that the entry point still exists is not the same as confirming deletion coverage, nor does it confirm when cleanup completes.

The starting point for investigating the ffmpeg issue is SOZI-223. That card calls for recovering the actual invocation from the most recent report of this issue and restoring the details of how it was invoked and the result the user saw. This requirement is narrower than "find the task name in the build file": what is needed is the selection outcome from an actual invocation, not a configuration location with a similar name. The earlier material mentioned "selection and fallback" but did not preserve snippets sufficient to reconstruct the exact arguments, binary location, or failure output; those details cannot be filled in from the title.

The distinction between "the earlier invocation" and "the current public entry point" must also be preserved here. The current public entry point describes where a capability can be accessed now; the earlier invocation concerns where to look to recover a historical action. Writing the earlier invocation's result into the entry-point documentation would make the entry point appear to promise details that have not yet been confirmed. Conversely, explaining the earlier invocation's fallback by pointing to the entry point's existing availability would also erase the difference in timing. These two kinds of material serve different purposes, even though both relate to export wrap-up.

The initial draft left a more tentative judgment: as long as export could continue to completion, encoder fallback could be considered sufficient. That judgment is retained as the position taken at the time, but is no longer used to determine whether the issue is closed. Export completion, whether resources are cleaned up, and which encoder the user ultimately used are distinct dimensions of the outcome. They may all be satisfied at once, or only one may be satisfied. Especially without an actual invocation result, "completion" cannot be used as a substitute for "fallback behaved as expected".

Likewise, "an encoding failure may leave intermediate artifacts behind" is not elevated into a causal description of the cleanup chain. It was a counterexample that prompted the two issues to be investigated together at the time, not a confirmed connection. If the same piece of runtime logic is later found to handle both directory deletion and encoder selection, that connection can be added to this page; until then, a shared release context cannot become evidence of a shared implementation.

The treatment of Gruntfile.js is therefore narrowed to two points. First, it remains a navigation point left by the earlier investigation, from which readers can verify task-loading relationships. Second, it is not the point responsible for Temporary Resource Cleanup or ffmpeg fallback. The `require("load-grunt-tasks")(grunt);` at the top of the file supports only the former judgment. Writing it up as the latter judgment would collapse build configuration, task discovery, and runtime behavior into a single layer, losing the very branch that needs to be investigated.

SOZI-221 and SOZI-223 do not serve the same documentation purpose either. The former preserves the entry point for Temporary Resource Cleanup and its still-unconfirmed aspects; the latter preserves the action of recovering the earlier invocation and filling in how it was invoked and the user-visible result. A status change on one card cannot supply missing facts for the other. If later material fills in only one side, only that side's paragraphs should be revised, without casually marking the other side as resolved.

The decision retained here is limited: do not elevate the task-loading relationships of Gruntfile.js into runtime responsibility; do not judge ffmpeg fallback by the status of the temporary-resource entry point; do not judge resource cleanup by the result of a single encoding attempt. This offers less of a neat conclusion than "the export issues have been handled together", but preserves the actual disagreement at the time: two issues whose names appear side by side have not yet been shown to share the same implementation.

Two pieces of original material are still missing. First, exactly what leftover resources the unconfirmed temporary-resource point concerns, and whether they fall within the cleanup scope described by the public entry point. Second, exactly what selection the most recent actual invocation referenced by SOZI-223 used, and what result the user actually saw after fallback. Until both are supplied, this page is suitable for explaining why the earlier investigation branched and for avoiding the mistake of treating build tasks as runtime responsibility; it is not suitable as an overall description of current export behavior.

The old combined investigation approach has not been deleted because it still explains why both terms appeared together in the historical record. But from this review onward, any new material should first be assigned to either "cleanup" or "selection and fallback". Discussion of them as a single chain should resume only when the material explicitly shows that both share the same piece of runtime logic.

# Localization Directory Dual-State Review

This record covers the incident in locales · Localization Catalog where the same object appeared in two states. The object came from the message catalog generated from the `.po` file and involved translation merging and pre-release language completeness. This directory has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria, and must not be conflated with other states in the main project.

The first observable symptom was that the same current entry point returned different current revisions at two points in time. On the first review, `repaint` differed from the old record. This was not merely a page-display issue, because the original record, recovery page, and unconfirmed cause were later retained separately; the content recorded in the three places was not collapsed into a single final judgment.

## Incident Timeline

- **Initial observation**: Reviewing the current entry point showed that `repaint` was inconsistent with the old record. The only thing initially confirmed was that the results at the two points in time differed; from this line alone, it was still impossible to determine whether the message catalog content had changed, the translation merge process had changed, or a different state had been used when reading the current entry point.
- **Preserve the original**: The review did not continue repeatedly retrying the same entry point; instead, it first preserved the version of `docs/adj-locales/incidents/locales-localization-catalog-two-states-for-one-object.md` from that time. Further retries were stopped to preserve the record from when the anomaly appeared; the retry result was not treated as overwriting the original incident.
- **Recovery check**: A later check confirmed that the preload bridge was recoverable. This only shows that the recovery path was available again; it cannot explain why different current revisions appeared at the two points in time, nor can the post-recovery result automatically be treated as the state observed the first time.
- **Handoff information added**: The on-call handoff added the version, request context, and stop conditions. The earlier record was missing a complete timestamp, so the missing actions still cannot be arranged into a continuous sequence.

## Impact and Assessment Changes

The confirmed impact is that locales · Localization Catalog left two different states at the current entry point. It affects the pre-release assessment of language completeness: looking only at the last green output could miss a discrepancy that had already been retained earlier. Existing records do not identify any broader set of affected objects, nor do they prove that all `.po` messages changed, so the incident cannot be generalized to mean that the entire localization directory is unusable.

Early on, the difference in `repaint` was the most immediately noticeable signal. That phenomenon did occur, but it was not the cause itself. During the review, there was no evidence to attribute the issue to a neighboring service; that speculation was not entered in the cause field. Later, the recovery page retained only confirmed recovery actions, the original record continued to retain the state observed at the time, and the unconfirmed cause was left open separately.

The only conclusion currently consistent with all these observations is: the same current entry point returned different current revisions at different times; there was at least one recoverable preload bridge state during that period; no causal relationship between the two has been established. The reason `camera path` changed is still unknown; successful recovery cannot substitute for this explanation, nor can it be used to infer whether translation merging has been completed.

This page is still referenced, mainly because it preserves a narrowly defined closeout sequence: when the message catalog window ends, save the final result first, then remove the temporary entry point. It does not make a release decision or determine on any maintainer's behalf whether the translations can ship.

An early version treated `locale catalogue`, `resource cleanup`, and `timeline` as terms that had to be checked when closing the window. The intent at the time was to prevent cleanup before samples were saved; that wording did not explain what to do if the two environments produced different results. The old passage is retained here to help identify records that still follow it:

> Do not clean up after seeing `resource cleanup`; stop if `timeline` does not appear.

This sentence may now be used only as a reminder to keep the environment intact. The absence of `timeline` is not enough to determine the window's status; the presence of `resource cleanup` does not mean the original input or last output can be deleted.

## Records to Capture Before Exiting

1. [ ] Find the entry for this window in `docs/adj-locales/release/locales-localization-catalog-exit-window-checklist.md` and save the original input, current revision, exit code, and final log segment.
2. [ ] Store the `.po` merge result generated for this window alongside the result of the last language completeness check. A success message in the log alone is not a substitute.
3. [ ] If the two environments produce different results, keep both results separately and stop comparing at the first divergence. The earlier review confirmed only that the results differed; the generation command had still not been found at the time, so neither environment's output can be recorded as the sole correct result.
4. [ ] Check whether translation merges are still writing to this window. While writes continue, do not remove the entry point or clean up the directory.

If item 2 is complete but item 3 is not, the window remains open. Here, "stop" means halting cleanup and release assessments, not deleting the materials already saved.

## Teardown Actions

Once you have confirmed there are no new merges, proceed in this order:

1. [ ] After saving the last visible result, remove the temporary entry point used for this review.
2. [ ] Recheck that the queue is no longer receiving work targeting that entry point.
3. [ ] Record that the exit action was performed, but do not change that line to report a successful release.

If removing the entry point fails, or if any of the exit code, original input, or last output is missing, stop before step 1. The recovery action did not leave a usable rerun record in the shared environment, so do not improvise recovery steps; preserve the directory and results as they are, and wait for the relevant maintainer to decide whether to open another window.

## A Later Divergence

A single-variable rerun was originally planned to hold `locales-localization-catalog`, the current entry point, and the command fixed, replacing only the current revision. Later, the original input had been rolled back, but the expiry action still pointed to the new artifact. This combination can no longer be handled directly using the old checklist's "save the last output, then release" rule: the old input and the new artifact do not belong to the same closeout set.

The required image of the old version was subsequently removed during cleanup, so the rerun was not completed. Without the old image, the only option is to retain the two existing results and the gaps that remained at the time; the new artifact must not be used to fill in a result for the old input.

- [ ] Is the original input still available?
- [ ] Have the last visible result and exit code been saved?
- [ ] Are the differing results from the two environments still saved separately?
- [ ] Has the temporary entry point been removed, or has the removal failure been explicitly recorded?

This discussion addressed how the team's public entry point should be maintained, not opening a separate path for any particular export format. The existing entry point remains centered on presentation-model; the alternative is to adjust the entry point and handoff relationship on the window side.

Decision: retain the current presentation-model entry point; the window-side adjustment is outside this round's approval scope. The reason is not that the window-side adjustment is necessarily ineffective, but that the existing materials cover only the public modules and reproducible export behavior. Every format should pass through the same presentation state and frame selection chain; if the entry point is moved to the window side first, ownership of the chain would be split before its actual impact was known.

When retaining the old entry point, it should be treated as a reversible arrangement rather than permanent ownership. If the actual impact, coordination arrangements, and rollback method for the window-side adjustment are added later, the options can be compared again; until then, do not copy presentation state or save a separate copy of the frame-selection rules just to make the handoff easier.

Reservation recorded at the time: it has not been confirmed whether the window-side entry point is merely a change in call location or will change how the flow from presentation state to frame selection works. This question was not closed in the meeting.
