# Public Entry Maintenance Decision Record

Public entry maintenance was treated at the time as a small handoff issue: who initiates the export and from where, and whether the window side should expose a more direct entry. After comparing the options in practice, the discussion did not treat it as simple interface placement. The existing entry is connected to presentation-model, followed by the presentation state and frame selection; as long as this relationship has not been clearly separated, changing the entry on the window side is not merely changing a call location.

The conclusion left by the initial draft still stands: this round retains the current presentation-model entry and does not approve moving the entry to the window side. This decision covers only the public modules and reproducible export behavior visible in the existing materials. It does not declare that the window side can never participate, nor does it establish the current file location as permanent ownership.

At the time, the meeting required documenting the actual impact, coordination arrangements, and a withdrawable old entry together. This record retains the decision itself and its reasons; if the handoff needs to be expanded further in response to window-side changes, see DOC-44. The two records serve different purposes: this one does not write the switching steps up as an established plan.

## The Two Paths Compared at the Time

The first path was to continue using presentation-model as the public entry. Its advantage is not that the name is more familiar, but that existing export behavior already starts from the same presentation state and passes through the same frame-selection relationship. Format differences may occur later, but separate state sources should not first branch off before the entry.

The second path was to adjust the window-side entry. The meeting did not reject this path as bad design; it was deferred because there was not enough material at the time to prove that, after the window-side adjustment, it would still pass through the same presentation state and the same frame-selection rules. If all we see is that the window can initiate an action, without seeing where the state and frame selection remain consistent, we cannot treat "can initiate" as "already integrated."

| Option | What could be confirmed at the time | Handling this round |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retain presentation-model entry | Existing public modules and reproducible export behavior were organized around the same presentation state and frame-selection chain | Continue retaining |
| Adjust the window-side entry | Could only confirm that it was an entry arrangement pending comparison; could not confirm the full state and frame-selection relationship | Not approved for now |

This table does not indicate a long-term priority between the two paths. It only explains why the meeting did not split the public entry first when the evidence was insufficient. When someone later reads that the "window-side adjustment was not approved," it should be understood as a judgment about scope, not as a technical rejection of the window object.

## Where the Decision Lands

The core constraint for retaining the entry is that every format must pass through the same presentation state and frame-selection chain. Here, "every format" refers to the public export path; it does not require every backend implementation to be identical. Formats may have their own output processes, but they cannot independently reacquire the presentation state or independently determine which frames should be selected.

This constraint provides entry maintenance with a clear decision point. If an adjustment still obtains content from the existing state and proceeds along the existing frame-selection relationship, it can be compared as a local adjustment in a later discussion. If it adds a duplicate state, independent filtering, or another set of default selections for the convenience of the window side, it has already exceeded the conditions for retaining the old entry this round.

The draft described "retaining the old entry" too much like a static directory selection, which is not accurate enough. What is actually retained is a relationship: public calls enter through presentation-model, then use the same presentation state and frame-selection chain. The entry name and file location may both change as maintenance proceeds; neither can replace this relationship.

Source tracing was once performed using `js/model/Presentation.js` and call names such as presentation and model. That check helped confirm the subject under discussion, but it cannot, on that basis, establish that file as the permanent ownership boundary for the public entry. The file was the location checked during the follow-up at the time; the decision focuses on the state and frame-selection relationship that the call must preserve.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Public export entry] --> B[presentation-model]
  B --> C[Presentation state]
  C --> D[Frame selection]
  D --> E[Output for each format]
```

The diagram does not draw the window as a parallel export chain in order to reflect this round's decision, not to assert that the window will never participate from now on. The window side can become an interaction entry point, but at the time it had not been proven that, after independently taking on public calls, it could still maintain the relationship shown in the diagram. It therefore was not approved as a replacement entry.

## Regarding Withdrawal of the Old Entry

Retaining the old entry does not mean locking it in place. The meeting required leaving a withdrawable old entry in place to avoid losing both the rollback point and the comparison object during a later adjustment. The prerequisite for withdrawal is not holding the same discussion again, but filling in the local facts missing from this round: the actual impact of the window-side change, its relationship to the presentation state, whether it continues to use the existing frame selection, and who will handle the unresolved parts during the handoff.

The original record did not make withdrawal an automatic action. The old entry cannot be considered ready for removal merely because the window side has a new control or a new call location. The old entry can be removed once the replacement relationship is confirmed; until then, it remains the known entry to the same chain. This wording is intentionally conservative because there was no complete window-adjustment plan available for item-by-item confirmation at the time.

Nor should the old entry instead be treated as a centralization point for format implementations. The decision protects the shared presentation state and frame selection; it does not require all format code to be concentrated in one module. If this distinction is omitted, future maintenance can easily conflate the "shared state chain" with "file centralization" as the same thing.

## Review Addendum

Later review did not broaden this decision. The review could still see export behavior organized around the presentation state and frame selection, and it still did not fill in the complete handoff relationship after the window adjustment. Therefore, the decision to retain the presentation-model entry remains applicable, but it still applies only to the scope that could be reviewed at that time.

The review also corrected an old wording that was easy to misread. The draft's "window-side adjustment" appeared to describe a change with a clearly defined boundary, but in fact it was only a set of arrangements brought in for comparison: it might involve the call entry, the handoff location, or the relationship between the window object and the existing model. There was not enough material to reduce these possibilities to one definite change, nor was there any reason to classify them all as the same risk.

Therefore, do not treat the "window side" as an inherently independent chain. It is merely an adjustment direction proposed in the discussion. The actual questions are: which presentation state does the adjustment read from, where is frame selection retained, and how does the format implementation enter the subsequent output? In this round's materials, only the existing entry can answer the first two questions; the third does not change this round's entry decision.

The review also preserved a boundary that had not been resolved at the time: the fact that a public module can be called does not mean that every invocation method has been compared. The existing materials support only that reproducible export behavior passes through a common chain; they do not constitute a description of every interaction form on the window side. Erasing this unknown would make the old decision appear broader than it actually was.

## Parts Not Yet Closed

The following points did not automatically receive answers merely because the old entry was retained:

- If the window side takes on a new handoff location, whether the presentation state is still provided by the same object;
- Whether frame selection will be reinterpreted on the window side or will continue to follow the existing selection relationship;
- When the old entry is withdrawn, who confirms that the replacement entry has covered the actual impact;
- Which differences in the format implementation are merely output differences, and which differences will in turn affect the public entry.

These points are not a request to immediately draw up another major plan; they limit how the conclusion on this page should be read. If one of them later has reviewable evidence, first compare the changes it causes to the shared state and frame-selection relationship, then decide whether to bring the window adjustment back into the decision.

The coordination arrangement is also valid only within this scope: what needs coordination is not every export implementation, but adjustments that may change the public entry, presentation state, or frame-selection relationship. Changes occurring only at the end of format output cannot be brought under this decision merely because they are "export-related"; conversely, a change that appears to be only a window handoff cannot bypass comparison just because it does not alter the output end.

## Filing Note

This record is still cited because it preserves why the window adjustment was not done first, not because it provides a map of all current entry points. The most useful part of the old conclusion is its constraint: the available evidence supports a shared presentation state and frame-selection chain; when the evidence is insufficient, do not split the public entry.

Some wording retains the context of that time, especially the wording that directly calls presentation-model the "current entry." Later maintenance should not treat this label as a permanent structural map; but until there is a clear record of the replacement relationship, it still indicates what this round chose to retain, what it deferred, and why the old entry must be capable of being withdrawn.

# export-runtime Entry-Point Code-Reading Notes

When tracing back from export-runtime, first use `export` appearing in Gruntfile.js as a search anchor, not as an ownership determination. Keep the original execution record alongside it to compare the names and order actually traversed at the time.

The initial assessment is that there are many files with the same name. Don't treat them as parallel entry points just because the filename, task name, or comment contains export. The path should retain only one direct caller; it must actually wire up the entry point for export-runtime. Only by following this call path do we reach the first real consumer involved in maintaining the team's public entry point.

```text
export-runtime
    |
    v
public entry point
    |
    v
one direct caller
    |
    v
the first real consumer involved in maintaining the team's public entry point
```

Here, "consumer" means the place that actually uses the entry point, not a file that declares the same name again. When you encounter a relationship that requires another owner to answer, stop there; don't add a guessed call edge for it.

At the time, it was still unconfirmed whether a second parallel path existed after the public entry point; this does not affect recording the first path already connected.

# export-runtime Entry Code-Reading Notes

This trace-back initially addressed just one easily confused question: when starting from export-runtime, the export name shown on the page does not automatically point to team-wide public-entry maintenance. Gruntfile.js was the starting point left at the time, and `export` was also a good-enough search anchor; neither can replace the actual call relationship. The original execution record is still retained for review because it shows which names were followed at the time, but it cannot by itself prove which file consumed the entry.

First split the search results into two buckets. The first bucket contains locations where export appears in a name, comment, or task description; these help reconstruct the work context at the time but do not enter the path graph. The second bucket contains call sites directly reachable from the public entry point. Only one direct caller from the second bucket was expanded further. The reason is simple: if several same-name paths are traced at once, the team-wide public-entry maintenance that appears later can look like it has multiple possible owners, and the reader no longer knows which location actually uses the entry.

The path retained here is as follows. The arrows show the reading direction verified in call order; they do not represent directory hierarchy or indicate that these objects are maintained by the same person.

```text
export-runtime
      |
      v
A callable location for the public entry point
      |
      v
One direct caller
      |
      v
The first actual consumer in team-wide public-entry maintenance
      |
      +--> Follow-on relationship requiring another owner's answer: stop here
```

Determining the "first actual consumer" is stricter than finding "a symbol with the same name." It must directly use the entry supplied by the previous step, or pass that entry into the next visible execution relationship. Merely re-exporting, mentioning export in a comment, or retaining a same-name string for a build task counts only as a signpost. This distinction is the core of this note; without it, the search results around Gruntfile.js mix the entry, aliases, and side paths together.

During review, the original execution record was not rewritten as a conclusion. The order in the record can help confirm sequence, but it is not the same as a call edge in the source; a name seen in the source does not mean runtime necessarily passes through it. Used together, the two let the person taking this over start from the same public entry and arrive at the same direct caller, rather than choose one arbitrarily from a string of search hits. If the run record and this reading direction disagree, return to the public entry and re-check the names; do not work backward from the later consumer to infer a seemingly plausible intermediate file.

Files with the same names that appear along the way remain in the margin of the note, but are not drawn into the main line. This does not deny that they may be related: some may belong to build preparation, some may simply be notes about the area around the export functionality, and some may only come into play on another entry point. The current path answers only "where team-wide public-entry maintenance first uses the entry in practice." It does not establish shared ownership for these files or write them up as unverified alternative paths.

When reading through it, stop at the following points in order: first confirm which public entry point export-runtime exposes; then inspect only one caller that connects directly to it; then, from that caller, find the first place that uses the entry in team-wide public-entry maintenance. If, after step three, it is necessary to determine who will take over public-entry maintenance next, leave the question as stated. Do not guess the downstream as another export name or connect a same-name file to an arrow just to complete the graph.

This follow-up check also corrected an ambiguous statement in the initial draft. The initial draft made "follow export to find the entry" sound like a full-text search; more precisely, export only gets you to the starting point, while direct call relationships filter the path. The original execution record is still useful for orientation, but it should not be used as a substitute for reading the calls.

The window discrepancy adjacent to this route is stored separately under DOC-46. That record can be used to understand why someone started tracing from the other-side entry at the time; this note does not expand on that discrepancy or fold it into the main line. The only unresolved item is the relationship after team-wide public-entry maintenance: only after the relevant owner answers can we decide whether to start another trace-back.

title: Public entry point maintenance deviation postmortem

versions.body:
# Postmortem: Public Entry Point Maintenance Discrepancy

This page records what happened during one maintenance window for the team's public entry points. After maintenance began, the visible results at the entry points did not match the original plan. When this was first noticed, all that could be confirmed was that the results differed; it was not possible to confirm which planned step had failed to take effect or to attribute the cause to a particular location. Here, results means the entry point state actually observed during the window, not an inference about maintenance actions or where responsibility lay. The scope of impact was not recorded as covering all entry points at the time; the response addressed only the part already observed.

## Changes During the Window

- Start of maintenance: Work proceeded according to the original plan, but the displayed entry point results did not match expectations. The initial discovery was recorded as an observed anomaly, not a settled conclusion about the cause.
- Coordination: The actual impact was recorded first, then temporary recovery was arranged. The coordinator, actual impact, and old entry points that could be withdrawn were not brought together in the initial record; they were only added to the postmortem later as control points, leaving gaps in the raw execution records.
- Temporary recovery: After the entry points were restored to a usable state, the team rechecked the results and continued closing out the maintenance window. Keep the recovery time as recorded during the response; do not rewrite the record as if the root cause had been known before recovery.
- After closeout: The visible results were temporarily in line with maintenance needs, but this only showed that the temporary measures had an observable effect at the time. It did not prove that all entry points had been affected in the same way or that every step in the original plan had taken effect.

Before temporary recovery, an anomaly at one entry point could not be taken to mean that the entire maintenance window had failed; the post-recovery checks also covered only the results being examined at the time, with no material showing that they covered all entry points.

## Response Decision at the Time

The response followed a "restore first, investigate later" approach: first return the public entry points to a usable state, then look back at the part of the maintenance plan that had not taken effect. This order explains why temporary recovery preceded confirmation of the cause. It did not identify a specific point of responsibility or turn the results of one window into present-day entry point rules. The raw execution records should still be retained to check the recovery time, actual impact, and temporary actions, rather than leaving only the statement "already restored."

## Remaining Boundaries

When reviewing the incident, keep three groups distinct: the entry points actually affected, the entry points used for temporary recovery, and the old entry points that could be withdrawn. Mixing them together obscures which parts the temporary actions covered and makes it impossible to tell whether the old entry points were still retained. The cause was still unresolved at the point in time covered by this page; there was also no further material on the specific scope of impact or the coordination process. Maintenance practices may have changed since then. This record preserves the account from the old window and cannot be treated directly as the current maintenance procedure.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Public Entry Point Result Discrepancies

The ticket says public entry point maintenance is complete, but the results can't be verified. First ask about the entry point used to call controller-storage; don't guess the cause from the results.

Results don't match
├─ Are both the entry point and the version in use specified?
│  ├─ No: stop; add the entry point name and version.
│  └─ Yes: use the same input to capture the raw execution records.
└─ Records differ: note the actual impact and any old entry points that can still be withdrawn; stop if a coordinator is needed.

# Troubleshooting tree for shared entry point result discrepancies

"Maintenance complete" only means someone took action; when results can't be verified, ask about each entry point separately. In one verification check, the calling entry point and version weren't both recorded, so the two results couldn't be compared directly.

```text
Results don't match
├─ Is the entry point used to call controller-storage specified?
│  ├─ No → Stop: add the entry point name and version used.
│  └─ Yes
│     └─ Are both sides using the same version?
│        ├─ No → Record the version difference; if the old entry point is still usable, mark the rollback location.
│        └─ Yes
└─ Get the raw execution records for the same input
   ├─ Records differ → Document the actual impact, coordinator, and rollback conditions for the old entry point; hand off here.
   └─ Records match → Stop: add records from the side displaying the result.
```

Record in one place which result was taken as completion, the scope of the impact, and who is coordinating. Don't use repeated reruns as a vote; reruns can't supply the missing entry point, version, or raw execution records.
